uncited: The PSNR Difference Metric for Ablation quantifies the performance degradation caused by removing a specific component from a rendering pipeline by comparing the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of a reduced configuration against a full baseline.

This metric sets itself apart from absolute metrics like [PSNR Metric Calculation](2742-psnr-metric-calculation.md) by providing a relative measure of loss, and from [3D Evaluation Metrics](2903-3d-evaluation-metrics.md) by focusing specifically on the delta between two specific configurations rather than a global scene score.
- **Inputs:** $\text{MSE}_{\text{config}}$ (Mean Squared Error of the ablated configuration), $\text{MSE}_{\text{full}}$ (Mean Squared Error of the full baseline method).
No complex data structures are required; the metric operates on scalar MSE values derived from pixel-wise comparisons.
Calculate the PSNR for the full method: $\text{PSNR}_{\text{full}} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\text{MAX}^2}{\text{MSE}_{\text{full}}}$.
Calculate the PSNR for the ablated configuration: $\text{PSNR}_{\text{config}} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\text{MAX}^2}{\text{MSE}_{\text{config}}}$.
Compute the difference $\Delta$ by subtracting the two PSNR values.
If $\text{MSE}_{\text{config}}$ is zero (perfect reconstruction), the logarithm is undefined.
The result is a single PSNR value (in dB) that facilitates the objective comparison of investigated compression techniques.
Similarly, BD-BR calculates the average bit-rate difference.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ relative to the number of pixels, as it operates on pre-computed scalar MSE values.
The calculation of the MSE itself is $O(N)$ where $N$ is the number of pixels.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ for the metric calculation itself.
It does not account for perceptual quality beyond MSE.
It is sensitive to the choice of the baseline "full" method.
- **When to use:** When performing ablation studies to quantify the contribution of specific components to the overall rendering quality.
- **When not to use:** When comparing methods with different bit depths or when perceptual metrics are more appropriate than MSE-based metrics.
The PSNR Difference Metric for Ablation is derived from the properties of the logarithmic scale used in PSNR calculations.
This allows for a clean comparison of error ratios without needing to specify the bit depth explicitly in the delta calculation.

The metric is particularly useful in the context of differentiable volume rendering and radiance-field optimization, where ablation studies are common to understand the impact of various optimization procedures and regularization losses.

Implementation for these metrics has been written in Excel VBA [S2].

The claim states that the implementation for the metrics (BD-PSNR and BD-BR) was written in Excel VBA. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states: 'Our particular implementation for calculating the BD-PSNR and BD-BR values was written in Excel VBA [58].' This directly confirms every part of the claim.
supported
To recover the error ratio from the difference, use the inverse relation [S1, unofficial]:

The evidence explicitly defines the difference Delta as 10 log10(MSE_full / MSE_config) and provides the inverse relation MSE_config / MSE_full = 10^(-Delta/10). It also confirms that the MAX term cancels out, making the metric independent of bit depth. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
It isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX), as MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the metric isolates the error ratio independent of bit depth (MAX) because MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference. The provided evidence explicitly confirms this: Source [S1] notes state 'This metric isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX), as MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference.' Furthermore, the passages demonstrate mathematically that when subtracting two PSNR values (which both contain MAX^2 in the numerator), the MAX^2 terms cancel out, leaving a ratio dependent only on MSE. Thus, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.
supported
A fixed dB difference always implies a fixed error ratio (e.g., 3 dB = 2x error), making it intuitive for ablation studies [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'A fixed gap always means a fixed ratio rather than a fixed amount' and provides the specific example that 'a difference of 10 × 0.30 = 3 dB corresponds to exactly a factor of two in error'. It also provides the formula to recover the error ratio from the dB difference. Therefore, the claim that a fixed dB difference implies a fixed error ratio is fully supported by the text.
supported

Originally designed within the Video Coding Experts Group (VCEG) – ITU SG 16 – for comparing video coding techniques, BD-PSNR measures the difference in compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality between two rate-distortion curves, represented by the area between the curves [S2].

The claim states that BD-PSNR was originally designed within the Video Coding Experts Group (VCEG) – ITU SG 16 – for comparing video coding techniques, and that it measures the difference in compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality between two rate-distortion curves, represented by the area between the curves. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly confirms all these points: it states that both BD-PSNR and BD-BR were 'originally designed within the Video Coding Experts Group (VCEG) – ITU SG 16 – for the comparison of various video coding techniques' and that 'BD-PSNR measures the difference in compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality between two rate-distortion curves, represented by the gray area as illustrated in Fig. 5.'
supported
It is not needed for the final calculation of $\Delta$ as it cancels out, provided both MSEs are computed using the same bit depth [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the bit depth (represented by MAX) is not needed for the final calculation of Δ because it cancels out, provided both MSEs are computed using the same bit depth. The evidence explicitly shows the mathematical derivation where MAX^2 appears in both PSNR terms and cancels out when subtracting them (Equation 17). Furthermore, the notes and text confirm that this metric isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX) because MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference.
supported

For example, a difference of 3 dB corresponds to exactly a factor of two in error ($10^{3/10} \approx 2$), and 6 dB corresponds to a factor of four, independent of the absolute PSNR values [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'a difference of 10 × 0.30 = 3 dB corresponds to exactly a factor of two in error, and 6 dB to a factor of four, independent of where on the scale the two values sit.' This directly supports the claim's assertion regarding the 3 dB and 6 dB factors and their independence from absolute PSNR values.
supported
The $\text{MAX}^2$ terms cancel out, simplifying the calculation to the ratio of the MSEs [S1, unofficial]:

The evidence explicitly states that the MAX^2 terms cancel out when calculating the difference in PSNR values, resulting in a formula that depends only on the ratio of the Mean Squared Errors (MSEs). Specifically, Equation (17) shows the cancellation of MAX^2, and the text confirms that this leaves a comparison of the error terms.
supported
The key property that the MAX term cancels out when subtracting two PSNR values was highlighted in architectural reviews of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that when subtracting two PSNR values, the MAX term cancels out because it appears as an identical numerator in both logarithmic terms. The text describes this as 'the key property of a logarithmic scale' where the quantity depending on an arbitrary choice (MAX) drops out entirely.
supported
BD-PSNR and BD-BR are metrics used to evaluate lossy compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality (BD-PSNR) or bit-rate (BD-BR) between two rate-distortion curves [S2].

The claim states that BD-PSNR and BD-BR are metrics used to evaluate lossy compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality (BD-PSNR) or bit-rate (BD-BR) between two rate-distortion curves. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly confirms this: it states that BD-PSNR measures the difference in compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality between two rate-distortion curves, and similarly, BD-BR represents the average relative difference in bit-rate between techniques. It also notes these are used for comparing video coding techniques (a form of lossy compression evaluation).
